course_description:
Models of action, perception, cognition and interaction in human-machine systems. Methods of interaction analysis and interaction representation. Human-machine system evaluation. Practical implementation. Introduction to user and use-centred design principles. Broader topics may include: societal considerations, groupware, multimedia, media perspectives.

DECO7250 gives students an introduction to human-computer interaction and interaction design including user experience, human-centred design, and identifying system requirements to support. Classes will be a mixture of lectures presenting the core concepts, and two-hour Studios during which students will work on activities that require the application of those core concepts.

The content of this course has been modified several times based on student feedback. The duration of the lecture has been extended, and group work has been reduced. We recently removed online quizzes, too. Lectures will involve active participation from attendees, and we will increasingly consider the changing role of UX in the human-computer interaction space.

AI tools may be used to support learning and task completion in this course, and the course provides guidance on appropriate use. Students are expected to apply judgement when using these tools, to check outputs carefully, and to ensure that all submitted work reflects their own understanding. Students are responsible for ensuring that any use of AI complies with academic integrity requirements and is appropriately acknowledged.

course_aims: This course provides students with an introduction to the theory and methods underlying Human-Computer Interaction. Students will gain experience in researching user needs and goals, then developing appropriately targeted design solutions to the needs and goals they have identified.

learning_outcomes.description: Analyse Human-Computer Interaction from historical and theoretical perspectives
Relate cognitive, social, behavioural, and emotional theories to the design of effective human-system interaction.
Analyse human-centred design issues by applying a range of design research methods, which involve the people from target user groups, in the process of interactive system design.
Apply HCI techniques and principles of user-interface design in the design of an interactive system.
Select and apply appropriate HCI evaluation (user and expert) techniques to evaluate interactive systems and analyse the results of those evaluation methods.
Apply HCI knowledge, in terms of system accessibility, within appropriate user-interface design for a broad range of user groups.
Develop collaborative design outcomes through both shared team and individual work.

Demonstrate an understanding of relevant HCI research by identifying, inspecting, and critiquing appropriate literature and with appropriate referencing [THIS LEARNING OBJECTIVE CONTRIBUTES TO AQF9 RESEARCH FOR MASTERS PROGRAMS]

assessment_details.task_description: In teams, you will work through a human-centred design process to propose a design for an interactive system (e.g., an app, web app, website, AR/VR app, or other system). A specific, detailed task sheet will be provided in class. The focus of this work is on the process that your team goes through to get to your final design. There will be specific touch points in studio sessions for you to get formative feedback en route to the final submission (in week 3 for topic selection and in week 5 for initial assumptions). Final submission of the whole project will be in Week 9. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Translation (MT) are emerging tools that may support students in completing this assessment task. Students may appropriately use AI and/or MT in completing this assessment task. Students must clearly reference any use of AI or MT in each instance. assessment_details.title: Interface Inquiry
assessment_details.task_description: Each student will appraise and assess an existing interface using a range of HCI theories and techniques. Students will (1) perform an expert evaluation/review, applying established HCI principles (e.g., Nielsen’s heuristics) to diagnose usability; and, (2) run a user-based evaluation, gathering direct feedback from users. Findings will be analysed and linked back to HCI theory, culminating in recommendations for future improvements. This approach develops essential evaluation skills and ensures accessibility considerations remain at the forefront. Students will produce a report that includes evidence of the inquiry, including a justification of the methods chosen and recommendations for what they would change and why.
